content:
**Landmarking** is a key technique for **dynamic prediction** in **time-to-event (survival) analysis**, often combined with **machine learning**. It enables updating individualized risk predictions as new longitudinal data arrives. [[1]](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/184/1/3/7056431)

### Core Concepts

**Survival analysis** (time-to-event analysis) models the time until an event of interest occurs (e.g., death, disease progression, failure), while handling censoring (when the event isn't observed for all subjects by study end).

**Dynamic prediction** updates survival probabilities over time for an individual based on their evolving covariates (e.g., biomarkers, lab results). Unlike static baseline predictions, it conditions on survival up to a current time and incorporates new information. [[2]](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Landmarking/vignettes/Landmarking.html)

**Landmarking** (introduced/promoted by van Houwelingen, 2007) is a practical approach for dynamic prediction: [[3]](https://www.efspi.org/documents/activities/international%20events/3heinputterpresentation.pdf)
- Select **landmark times** (e.g., 0, 6 months, 1 year, etc.).
- At each landmark *s*, create a dataset of individuals still event-free ("at risk") up to *s*.
- Use covariates measured up to *s* (often summarized, e.g., last observation carried forward — LOCF — or via mixed-effects models for full history).
- Fit a survival model (e.g., Cox) for the probability of the event in a fixed window (e.g., next *w* years) from *s*.
- This creates "partly conditional" predictions that update dynamically.

**Advantages**:
- Computationally simpler and more robust than **joint models** (which simultaneously model longitudinal trajectories and survival, but can be complex with many markers).
- Flexible for high-dimensional or machine learning integration.
- Avoids some assumptions of joint models. [[4]](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12874-022-01660-3)

**Limitations**:
- Uses only data from at-risk individuals at each landmark (less efficient than joint models in theory).
- Choice of landmarks and summarization of history matters. [[5]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5957493/)

### Integration with Machine Learning

Landmarking pairs well with ML for better handling of complex, high-dimensional, or nonlinear relationships:

- **Super Learner** ensembles (e.g., combining Cox, random forests, boosting) applied at landmarks via discrete-time survival formulation. [[6]](https://researchonline.lshtm.ac.uk/id/eprint/4657641/)
- **Gradient boosting** (e.g., Landmarking-Gradient Boosting Models — LGBM) for nonparametric dynamic prediction. [[7]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12513103/)
- **Random Survival Forests** or other tree-based methods.
- Packages: R `Landmarking`, `dynamicLM`, `landmaRk` GitHub repo. [[2]](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Landmarking/vignettes/Landmarking.html)

These often outperform traditional Cox landmarking in predictive accuracy (e.g., time-dependent AUC) while remaining interpretable. [[8]](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1504535/pdf)

### Threshold Crossing and First-Hitting-Time (FHT) Models

**Threshold crossing** (or **first-hitting-time** models) offers an alternative/complementary framework to proportional hazards (e.g., Cox):

- Model the event as the first time a latent stochastic process (e.g., Wiener/Brownian motion, gamma) crosses a boundary/threshold.
- Natural for processes that "degrade" over time until failure (e.g., biomarker reaching a critical level, device wear).
- **Threshold regression** links covariates to process parameters (starting level, drift, volatility). [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-hitting-time_model)

**Dynamic/landmarking extensions**:
- Longitudinal data can update the process parameters at landmarks.
- Useful when proportional hazards assumptions fail.
- ML boosting versions exist for high-dimensional FHT. [[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10006065/)

FHT provides an intuitive mechanistic view (underlying process hitting threshold) vs. landmarking's more empirical, data-driven updating. They can be combined in hybrid approaches.

### Practical Workflow Example

1. Define landmarks and prediction window *w*.
2. For each landmark *s*:
   - Subset at-risk data.
   - Summarize covariates up to *s*.
   - Fit model (Cox, ML ensemble, or FHT).
3. For a new patient at current time *s*, predict P(event in [*s*, *s*+*w*] | survived to *s*, covariates).
4. Update as new data arrives.

**Evaluation**: Time-dependent AUC (tdAUC), Brier score, calibration at landmarks. [[11]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11876041/)

### Applications

- Clinical: Updating prognosis in cancer, transplant, Alzheimer's (ADNI data), chronic diseases with serial biomarkers.
- Reliability engineering: Time to equipment failure.
- Competing risks or multi-state extensions exist.

For implementation, start with the R `Landmarking` vignette or papers by Tanner et al. (Super Learner + landmarking) and van Houwelingen/Putter. Recent work (2025) emphasizes ML hybrids for superior performance. [[1]](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/184/1/3/7056431)

This framework is active in research, balancing flexibility, performance, and interpretability for real-time personalized predictions.

sources.description:
### Landmarking

The landmarking approach is a method for dynamic prediction. The landmarking approach uses predefined prediction times (landmark times) for dynamic prediction. The time points were chosen from a prediction interval , where is the maximum prediction time of interest. To dynamically predict the probability of survival in the next years, given that the subjects have survived until time , at each landmark time , a survival model is fitted to the subjects within the risk set. The subjects are included in the risk set if they have not experienced the event or have been censored until the landmark time , and the subjects who did not experience the event until the time horizon are considered administratively censored at . [...] The gradient boosting method is an ensemble nonparametric machine learning algorithm widely applied in various fields, including survival analysis [28, 29]. Gradient boosting begins with a weak learner and incrementally improves its performance. In 2020, a study investigated dynamic survival prediction for binary data via a combination of the landmarking approach and a machine learning technique known as the super learner . Another study investigated dynamic survival prediction in the presence of longitudinal markers via a combination of the random forest algorithm with the landmarking approach . The main limitation of the random forest algorithm is that the large number of trees can slow the prediction process . The purpose of our study is to develop dynamic prediction models via a [...] One of the common methods for the dynamic prediction of survival in the presence of longitudinal markers is the joint modeling method [8, 11]. Joint models incorporate a sub-model for survival and a sub-model for longitudinal marker trends, linking these two components through a shared parameter . Calculating conditional survival probabilities in joint models involves numerical integration, which is often computationally intensive . A simpler approach for dynamic prediction in the presence of longitudinal markers is the landmarking approach. In the landmarking method, at each landmark time, a survival model is fitted to individuals who are at risk, utilizing patient information available up to that specific landmark time .
